sections.section_title: Liberation through Dīkṣā and the Six Paths (Ṣaḍadhvā)
sections.content: This section, marked by '(1)', introduces the core ideology of Śaiva-siddhānta: final liberation is secured not by knowledge (jñāna) but through the grace of Godhead via the initiatory rite of dīkṣā. Dīkṣā's immediate purpose is the purification of the paths (adhva-saṁśuddhi), which leads to the elimination of the mundane condition. The chapter quotes the Rauravāgama to support this. It then explains the concept of the six 'paths' (ṣaḍadhvā), a map of reality common to Kāśmīra and South Indian Śaivism. These paths are not just philosophical but are a practical religious method to be experienced within oneself (piṇḍāṇḍa). The six paths are divided into two groups of three: the expressive (vācaka) and the expressed (vācya). The first three (vācaka) are: (1) mantrādhvā (path of mantras), (2) padādhvā (path of words, based on the vyoma-vyāpi-padamantra), and (3) varṇādhvā (path of letters/phonemes). The latter three (vācya) are: (4) bhuvanādhvā (path of worlds/planes of experience, 224 in number), (5) tattvādhvā (path of fundamental categories, 36 in number), and (6) kalādhvā (path of five aspects that pervade the others). The section then focuses on the 36 tattvas, which include the 25 of classical Sāṁkhya (classified as 'impure' or aśuddha) plus eleven additional Śaiva tattvas. These eleven are: Śiva, Śakti, Sadā-śiva, Īśvara, Śuddha-vidyā, Māyā, Kalā, Vidyā, Rāga, Kāla, and Niyati. The tattvas are further grouped into 'objective' (bhogya-kāṇḍa), 'impelling' (preraka-kāṇḍa), and 'subjective' (bhojayitṛ-kāṇḍa). The paths are also divided into 'pure' (śuddha), where Śiva is directly responsible, and 'impure' (aśuddha), where māyā is the cause and Śiva is indirectly responsible through the vidyeśvaras. The distinction between Parama-śiva (transcendental) and Śiva-tattva (a category) is made. Further subdivisions like 'pure-and-impure' (śuddhāśuddha) are also mentioned. The text then correlates the five kalās with the 36 tattvas. Śiva's five functions (kṛtya-pañcaka) are listed: creation (sṛṣṭi), preservation (sthiti), dissolution (saṁhāra), veiling (tirobhāva), and grace (anugraha). The 'pure' division consists of five successive categories: Śiva-tattva, Śakti-tattva (also known as 'nāda'), Sadāśiva (where subject dominates object), Īśvara (where subject and object are equal), and Śuddha-vidyā (where object dominates subject).
sections.summary: This section establishes that in Śaiva Siddhānta, liberation is achieved through the grace-bestowing ritual of dīkṣā, which purifies the six paths (ṣaḍadhvā). It details these six paths and focuses on the 36 tattvas (categories of existence), which subsume the Sāṁkhya system within a larger theistic framework. It introduces the classification of paths and tattvas into 'pure' and 'impure' categories and describes Śiva's five cosmic functions and the emanation of the five 'pure' tattvas.

sections.section_title: Māyā, Pañca-Kañcuka, and the Five Kalās
sections.content: This section, marked by '(2)', introduces the concept of mahā-māyā or bindu as the substantial cause of the 'pure' division, distinct from the māyā of the 'impure' division. Mahā-māyā is described as Śiva's 'assumptive power' (parigraha-śakti), which is eternal and activated by his will. It is also identified with Kuṇḍalinī energy. From the 'impure māyā' emerge its immediate aids, the five sheaths (pañca-kañcuka) that limit the individual soul (puruṣa). These are: kalā (limited capacity for action), niyati (principle of necessity/destiny), kāla (time), vidyā (limited knowledge), and rāga (desire/attachment). The individual soul, when enveloped by these five sheaths, is called puruṣa. Its objective counterpart is prakṛti, which provides the soul with a body, mind, and senses. The soul (puruṣa) is distinct from the pure soul; it is the soul in a state of bondage, inclined towards prakṛti due to the five coverings and the five kleśas (from Yoga-sūtra). The text explains that there are 224 planes of existence (bhuvanas) in total across the various divisions. The concept of kalā as a 'fragment' is elaborated, and the five kalās are enumerated in ascending order: (1) Nivṛtti (withdrawal), (2) Pratiṣṭhā (establishment), (3) Vidyā (cognition), (4) Śānta (tranquil), and (5) Śāntyatīta (transcending tranquility). Their correspondence to the elements, the tattvas, and regions of the individual's body is detailed. The section concludes by stating that at the time of great dissolution (mahā-pralaya), only three categories remain distinct: Śiva, puruṣa (the soul), and māyā. The soul is entirely dependent on Śiva for both bondage and freedom.
sections.summary: This section differentiates between mahā-māyā (or bindu), the cause of the pure creation, and māyā, the cause of the impure creation. It details the five 'sheaths' (pañca-kañcuka) that emanate from māyā, which limit the individual soul and define its state as puruṣa. The five cosmic aspects, or kalās, are described, linking the macrocosmic structure of reality to the microcosmic individual. Finally, it affirms the eternal existence of Śiva, the soul (puruṣa), and māyā as three distinct principles.

sections.section_title: The Triad of Pati, Paśu, and Pāśa
sections.content: Marked by '(3)', this section discusses the most important doctrine of Śaiva-siddhānta: the tripartite view of reality as Pati (the Godhead), Paśu (the fettered individual soul), and Pāśa (the phenomenon of bondage). This triad is presented as philosophically valid and religiously relevant. The terminology is ancient, possibly predating classical Śaivism and characteristic of the Pāśupata school. Pati refers to Śiva as the 'master' or 'protector' and includes Śakti. Paśu, literally 'beast', refers to the individual soul which is ignorant, bound by fetters, and harassed by limitations. It is distinguished from the liberated and the initiated (dīkṣita). The inherent nature of the soul is pure and pervasive, but its association with māyā makes it impure and fragmented ('aṇu'). In this state, it is an agent (kartā) and enjoyer (bhoktā) of its actions. Pāśa, the bonds, are generally of three kinds: (1) Āṇava-mala (innate impurity, like husk on rice), which limits the soul's powers; (2) Karma (residual action-complex); and (3) Māyeya (bondage of māyā, causing wrong identification). Some sources, like Bhoja-deva, define the bonds as a five-fold group (arthapañcaka), adding 'jagat' (the world created from māyā) and 'tirodhānakarī śakti' (Śiva's power of obscuration) to the primary three. Śiva's obscuring power is a 'bond' that keeps the world process going, forcing the soul to participate. Bound individuals are classified into two types: the worldly (paśus proper) and the seekers (dīkṣitas). The seekers are further divided into three grades based on their bondage: (1) Sakala (fettered by all three bonds: mala, karma, māyā), (2) Pralayākala (fettered by two: mala and karma), and (3) Vijñānakala (fettered by only one: āṇava-mala). The text describes the spiritual progression and the form in which Śiva's grace operates for each class. These three stages are correlated with states of consciousness: jāgrat (waking), svapna (dream), and suṣupti (deep sleep). Beyond these lies the transcendental stage of turīya (inhabited by mantras, mantreśvaras, etc.) and the final state of turīyātīta, which is the category of Śiva, where the soul becomes like Śiva.
sections.summary: This section explains the fundamental Śaiva Siddhānta triad of Pati (Godhead), Paśu (soul), and Pāśa (bondage). It defines each term, detailing the nature of the soul's bondage through three primary fetters (āṇava-mala, karma, māyeya) and sometimes two additional ones. It classifies souls into three hierarchical categories (Sakala, Pralayākala, Vijñānakala) based on the extent of their bondage, linking these stages to states of consciousness and the progressive path to liberation (Śiva-sāyujya).

sections.section_title: The Threefold Manifestation of Śiva: Niṣkala, Sakala-Niṣkala, Sakala
sections.content: Marked by '(4)', this section outlines another tripartite scheme of reality based on aspects (kalā): (1) Niṣkala (totally un-aspected), (2) Sakala-niṣkala (aspected as well as unaspected), and (3) Sakala (aspected). These correspond respectively to Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Maheśa. The Niṣkala Śiva is the supreme, transcendental, undifferentiated reality. For the sake of creation and devotees, Śiva, by his will, differentiates himself into five primordial powers (Śaktis): parā-śakti, ādi-śakti, icchā-śakti, jñāna-śakti, and kriyā-śakti. The Sakala-niṣkala phase involves the combination of these aspected powers with the unaspected Śiva principle, creating five processes or modes of being called 'sādas'. This term emphasizes the integration of tattva (reality) and mūrti (form), like the relationship between soul and body. The five sādas are: (i) Śiva-sāda, (ii) amūrta-sāda (uncrystallized), (iii) mūrta-sāda (crystallized), (iv) kartṛ-sāda (performing/agent), and (v) karma-sāda (action). Each sāda is described in detail, including its corresponding Śakti, deity, and form (often a liṅga with or without an iconic representation). For example, the karma-sāda manifests as a liṅga on a pedestal, symbolizing the universe, and its iconic form is five-faced. The Sakala division is that of Maheśa, produced from the karma-sāda. This is the fully aspected phase that comprehends creation, preservation, and dissolution. In this phase, Śiva has twenty-five 'sportive forms' (līlā-mūrti), such as Naṭarāja, Gaṅgādhara, and Dakṣiṇāmūrti. The text describes the original Maheśa-mūrti form (as Rudra) and the origin of other gods like Brahmā and Viṣṇu from him. The section concludes by stating that only the universe brought into being by the karma-sāda (the Sakala phase) is available for concrete visualization, while the other four sādas are for the contemplation of adepts.
sections.summary: This section presents a different tripartite classification of Śiva's reality: Niṣkala (unmanifest), Sakala-niṣkala (partially manifest), and Sakala (fully manifest). It details the emergence of five primordial Śaktis from the Niṣkala Śiva. The Sakala-niṣkala phase is explained through the unique concept of the five 'sādas', which are modes of reality integrating the formless and the formed. Finally, the Sakala phase is identified with Maheśa and his twenty-five iconic, sportive forms (līlā-mūrti) that constitute the manifest universe.

chapter_summary: Chapter V, titled 'ŚAIVA SIDDHĀNTA (2)', provides a detailed exposition of the core tenets of Śaiva Siddhānta philosophy. It begins by establishing that liberation is achieved not through knowledge alone but through divine grace actualized in the initiatory rite of dīkṣā. The chapter lays out the comprehensive cosmological and soteriological map of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvā) and the thirty-six categories of existence (tattvas), which expand upon the Sāṁkhya system. A central theme is the fundamental triad of reality: Pati (Godhead), Paśu (the individual soul), and Pāśa (the bonds of māyā, karma, and āṇava-mala). The text meticulously classifies souls based on the number of bonds that fetter them (Sakala, Pralayākala, Vijñānakala) and correlates these stages with different states of consciousness. Finally, it presents a hierarchical model of Śiva's manifestations—from the utterly transcendent and unaspected (Niṣkala) to the partially manifest (Sakala-Niṣkala) forms of Sadāśiva expressed through the five 'sādas', and culminating in the fully aspected, iconic forms (Sakala) of Maheśa, including his twenty-five sportive līlā-mūrtis. The chapter synthesizes metaphysical doctrine with practical religious concepts, emphasizing the journey of the soul from bondage to liberation through divine grace and ritual.
key_arguments: Final release in Śaiva Siddhānta is secured not by knowledge (jñāna) alone, but by the grace of Godhead through the initiatory rite of dīkṣā.
Reality is structured into six paths (ṣaḍadhvā) and thirty-six tattvas, providing a comprehensive map for the practitioner that is both phenomenological and ontological.
The core doctrine is the tripartite classification of reality into Pati (Godhead), Paśu (fettered soul), and Pāśa (bondage), which are the fundamental components of existence.
The soul is intrinsically pure, but its powers are obscured by three primary bonds (mala, karma, māyā), and its liberation consists in the removal of these bonds through grace.

Śiva actively engages with the world through a spectrum of manifestations, from the formless (niṣkala) to the fully formed (sakala), in order to facilitate both cosmic processes and the soul's liberation.
key_takeaways: The ritual of dīkṣā is central and indispensable for salvation in Śaiva Siddhānta.
The philosophical system is highly structured, integrating Sāṁkhya categories into a broader theistic framework dominated by Śiva.
The concept of bondage (Pāśa) is multifaceted, including an innate impurity (āṇava-mala), the law of action (karma), and the power of illusion (māyā).
Śiva's grace is a key doctrine, acting not only as a liberating force (anugraha) but also as a veiling power (tirobhāva) that enables worldly experience.
The classification of souls (Sakala, Pralayākala, Vijñānakala) provides a clear framework for understanding different levels of spiritual evolution.

historical_figures.name: Aghora-śiva
historical_figures.significance: Commented on Bhoja-deva's Tattva-prakāśa. His interpretations on the nature of 'pāśa' and Śiva are cited.

historical_figures.name: Bhoja-deva
historical_figures.significance: Author of Tattva-prakāśa, a foundational text of Śaiva Siddhānta. His definitions of 'pāśa' are discussed.

historical_figures.name: Bhaṭṭa-Vāmadeva
historical_figures.significance: Author of 'Janma-maraṇa-vicāra', quoted for the definition of 'svatantrya' as 'ānandaśaktiḥ'. Associated with Kashmir Śaivism.

historical_figures.name: Kṣemarāja
historical_figures.significance: A major figure in Kashmir Śaivism, his commentary on Bhaṭṭa-nārāyaṇa's Stava-cintāmaṇai is cited.

historical_figures.name: Bhaṭṭa-nārāyaṇa
historical_figures.significance: Author of 'Stava-cintāmaṇai', quoted regarding Śiva's power to undo the snares of māyā.

historical_figures.name: Rāma-kaṇṭha
historical_figures.significance: Commentator on 'Mataṅga-pārameśvara', quoted on how pure knowledge uproots ignorance when Śiva's energy descends.

historical_figures.name: Jayaratha
historical_figures.significance: Commentator on Abhinavagupta's 'Tantrāloka', cited for his alternative view of 'mala' as ignorance rather than a substance.

historical_figures.name: Ananta
historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as the head of the vidyeśvaras, who are responsible for the 'impure' creation. Also listed as one of the eight forms of Śiva in the Īśvara category.

geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as a region where a form of Śaivism prevailed that shared the concept of the six 'paths' (ṣaḍadhvā) with the Southern Siddhānta school.
geographic_locations.significance: A major center for the development of non-dualistic Śaiva traditions.

geographic_locations.context: Identified as the region where the form of Śaivism known as 'siddhānta' prevails.
geographic_locations.significance: The heartland of the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta tradition.

geographic_locations.context: Cited as the publication location for the 'Kaśmir-series of texts and studies' which published editions of Bhaṭṭa-Vāmadeva's and Kṣemarāja's works.
geographic_locations.significance: A modern center of learning in Kashmir.

geographic_locations.context: Cited as the publication location for a volume of the Rauravāgama by the French Institute of Pondicherry.
geographic_locations.significance: A notable center for Indological and manuscript research.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: The central rite in Śaiva-siddhānta through which a practitioner receives divine grace and is set on the path to liberation.
Contrasted with dīkṣā; knowledge alone is not sufficient for final release.
The immediate purpose of dīkṣā, which involves purifying the six paths of reality.
The six-fold map of reality, comprising mantras, words, letters, worlds, tattvas, and kalās.
The 36 fundamental categories that constitute all of reality, from the gross elements to the supreme Śiva.
Used in multiple senses: one of the pañca-kañcuka (limited power of action), the five cosmic aspects (Nivṛtti, etc.), and the aspects of Śiva's manifestation (niṣkala, sakala).
The first category of the fundamental triad; the Godhead, Śiva.
The second category of the triad; the individual soul bound by impurities.
The third category of the triad; the phenomenon of bondage, comprising mala, karma, and māyā.
The primordial, innate impurity that clouds the soul's consciousness and limits its powers, causing a sense of imperfection.
The bond consisting of the accumulated potencies of past actions, which determines future experiences.
The material cause of the 'impure' universe and the bond that provides the soul with a body and world for its experience.
One of Śiva's five functions; the power that conceals the soul's true nature, enabling it to experience the world.
One of Śiva's five functions; the liberating power that reveals the soul's true nature and grants release.
The highest, transcendent, and formless aspect of Śiva.
The fully manifest, formed aspect of Śiva (as Maheśa). Also refers to the class of souls bound by all three pāśas.
The intermediate aspect of Śiva (as Sadāśiva) which is both with and without form.
A concept peculiar to Śaiva-siddhānta describing the five modes of reality in the sakala-niṣkala phase, representing the integration of tattva and mūrti.

cross_references.target: A chapter or entry on DĪKŚĀ

cross_references.reference_text: the same as we find in Yoga-sūtra

quotations.quote: दीक्षया मुच्यते देही त्रिविधाद् भवबन्धनात्। सा दीक्षा चाध्वसंशुद्धिः सा चाध्वा ष‌ड्विधः स्मृतः ॥
quotations.context: States that through dīkṣā the embodied soul is freed from the threefold bondage of existence. This dīkṣā is the purification of the paths, and that path is said to be sixfold. Used to introduce the central concepts of the chapter.

quotations.quote: पंचकंचुसंयुक्तः प्रकृतिं भोक्तुमुद्यतः । अविद्यादिसमायुक्तः पुरुषः परिकीर्तितः ॥
quotations.context: Defines 'puruṣa' (person/individual soul) as that which, equipped with the five coverings (pañca-kañcuka) and associated with ignorance, proceeds to experience the objective world (prakṛti).

quotations.quote: पंचविधं तत्कृत्यं सृष्टिस्थितिसंहृतितिरोभावाः। तद्वदनुग्रहकरणं प्रोक्तं सततोदितस्यास्य ।।
quotations.context: Lists the five functions (kṛtya-pañcaka) of the ever-risen Lord (Śiva): creation, preservation, dissolution, obscuration, and the act of grace.
States the established triad: the one to be bound (pāśya/paśu), the binder (pāśayitā/pati), and the bonds (pāśāḥ).

quotations.source: Bhaṭṭa-Vāmadeva's Janma-maraṇa-vicāra, Śrīnagar, Kaśmir-series of texts and studies, 1918
quotations.context: Defines independence (svātantrya) as the power of bliss (ānanda-śakti), in the context of describing Śiva-tattva.

quotations.quote: The chapter includes numerous other Sanskrit quotations from sources like the Svāyambhuva-sūtra, Rauravāgama, Mataṅga-pārameśvara, Pañca-sādākhya-vidhi, and others, each used to substantiate specific doctrinal points about the tattvas, pati-paśu-pāśa, the classes of souls, and the manifestations of Śiva.
quotations.context: These quotes serve as scriptural proof-texts for the philosophical arguments being presented throughout the chapter.

controversial_points: The nature of 'mala' (primordial impurity) is debated. The main text presents it as substantial (dravya-rūpa), but notes that commentator Jayaratha regards it as a form of ignorance, which is eliminated when knowledge dawns (p. 91).

The exact composition of the 'pāśas' (bonds) can vary. The text presents the common triad (mala, karma, māyā), a four-fold scheme from Bhoja-deva (mala, karma, māyā, śiva-śakti), and a five-fold scheme (mala, karma, māyā, jagat, tirodhānakarī śakti) (pp. 92-93).

alternative_viewpoints.viewpoint: Location of the Five Kalās in the Body
alternative_viewpoints.description: The Suprabheda text maps the five kalās to regions from the feet to the top of the head. The Rauravāgama, however, locates them differently: in the heart, head, neck, palate, eyebrows, and top of the head (p. 84).

Some texts introduce the concept of 'mahā-māyā' (great power of production) or 'bindu' in the 'pure division' between Śiva-tattva and his śakti, while others may not make this specific distinction (p. 80).
The 'impure' division of paths is sometimes further divided into 'pure-and-impure' (śuddhāśuddha) and 'impure' (aśuddha), creating a more granular classification (p. 75).
